```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
library(flextable)
library(ftExtra)
library(dplyr)

# Source all data prep and model results
source("analyses.R")

### Table helpers ###

set_flextable_defaults(font.family = "Calibri", font.size = 9,
                       padding.top = 3, padding.bottom = 3,
                       border.color = "black")

# Column alignment given as one letter per column (e.g. lrlr)
align_columns <- function(ft, spec) {
  key  <- c(l = "left", r = "right", c = "center")
  cols <- strsplit(spec, "")[[1]]
  for (a in unique(cols)) ft <- align(ft, j = which(cols == a), align = key[[a]], part = "all")
  ft
}

# Journal-style table
base_table <- function(df, spec) {
  ft <- flextable(df)
  ft <- theme_booktabs(ft)
  ft <- colformat_md(ft)
  ft <- align_columns(ft, spec)
  ft <- valign(ft, valign = "bottom", part = "header")
  set_table_properties(ft, layout = "autofit",
                       width = if (knitr::is_html_output()) 0.6 else 1)
}

# Write the numbered title (same style as figures), then the table
finish_table <- function(ft, title) {
  title_block(title)
  flextable_to_rmd(ft)
}

# Order of tables and figures, numbered within each kind
OUTPUTS <- c(
  demographics = "Table",
  en_models = "Table",
  en_importance = "Figure",
  sfc_em = "Figure",
  lme = "Table",
  motion = "Supplementary Table",
  flow = "Supplementary Figure",
  en_features = "Supplementary Table",
  en_svm = "Supplementary Table",
  en_svm_importance = "Supplementary Figure",
  lme_s400 = "Supplementary Table"
)

# Start figure numbering at 2 and supplementary tables at 2
FIRST_NUMBER <- c(Figure = 2, `Supplementary Table` = 2)

# Numbered label for text and captions
ref <- function(key) {
  kind <- OUTPUTS[[key]]
  first <- if (kind %in% names(FIRST_NUMBER)) FIRST_NUMBER[[kind]] else 1
  number <- match(key, names(OUTPUTS)[OUTPUTS == kind]) + first - 1
  paste0(kind, " ", number)
}

# Title
caption_title <- function(key, text) sprintf("**%s.** %s", ref(key), text)

# Absolute path so images render in both HTML and Word
FIG_DIR <- normalizePath("figures")

# Title above any table or figure
title_block <- function(title) cat("\n\n::: {.fig-title}\n", title, "\n:::\n\n", sep = "")

# Numbered title above a figure
fig_title <- function(key, text) title_block(caption_title(key, text))

# One centered image
single_figure <- function(file, width) {
  cat(sprintf("\n\n::: {.fig-single}\n![](%s){width=%s}\n:::\n\n", file.path(FIG_DIR, file), width))
}

# Italicize heading rows and indent the rest by level
style_rows <- function(ft, labels, is_heading, level) {
  ft <- compose(ft, i = which(is_heading), j = 1, value = as_paragraph(as_i(labels[is_heading])))
  for (l in 1:2) ft <- padding(ft, i = which(level == l), j = 1, padding.left = 18 * l)
  ft
}

# Table whose heading rows have empty data cells (from the Python table scripts)
render_sectioned_table <- function(df, spec, title) {
  is_heading <- df[[2]] == ""
  ft <- style_rows(base_table(df, spec), df[[1]], is_heading, ifelse(is_heading, 0, 1))
  for (i in which(is_heading)) ft <- merge_h_range(ft, i = i, j1 = 1, j2 = ncol(df))
  finish_table(ft, title)
}

### Formatting helpers ###

# β coefficient
fmt_b <- function(x) formatC(as.numeric(x$coef), format = "f", digits = 4)

# 95% CI as "lo to hi" for inline text
fmt_ci_text <- function(x) {
  ci <- as.numeric(x$ci)
  paste0(formatC(ci[1], format = "f", digits = 4), " to ",
         formatC(ci[2], format = "f", digits = 4))
}

# 95% CI as "lo-hi" for table cells
fmt_ci_dash <- function(x) {
  ci <- as.numeric(x$ci)
  paste0(formatC(ci[1], format = "f", digits = 4), "-",
         formatC(ci[2], format = "f", digits = 4))
}

# "Coef (lo-hi)" combined cell for tables
fmt_coef_ci <- function(x) paste0(fmt_b(x), " (", fmt_ci_dash(x), ")")

# p-value for inline text: returns "=0.0450" or "<0.0001"
fmt_p <- function(p, digits = 4) {
  p <- as.numeric(p)[1]
  if (is.na(p))       return("=NA")
  if (p < 10^-digits) return(paste0("<", formatC(10^-digits, format = "f", digits = digits)))
  paste0("=", formatC(p, format = "f", digits = digits))
}

# p-value for table cells, with significance stars
fmt_p_star <- function(p, digits = 4) {
  p <- as.numeric(p)[1]
  if (is.na(p)) return("")
  base <- formatC(p, format = "f", digits = digits)
  if      (p < 0.001) paste0(base, "***")
  else if (p < 0.01)  paste0(base, "**")
  else if (p < 0.05)  paste0(base, "*")
  else                base
}

# FDR p-value for inline text
fmt_p_fdr <- function(x) fmt_p(x$p_fdr)

# Inline stats for one LME model
fmt_stats <- function(x) {
  paste0("β=", fmt_b(x), ", 95% CI ", fmt_ci_text(x), ", p", fmt_p(x$p_value), ", pFDR", fmt_p_fdr(x),
         ", marginal r²=", fmt_r2m(x), ", conditional r²=", fmt_r2c(x))
}

# Marginal / conditional R² from LME models
fmt_r2m <- function(x) formatC(as.numeric(x$marginal_r2),    format = "f", digits = 4)
fmt_r2c <- function(x) formatC(as.numeric(x$conditional_r2), format = "f", digits = 4)

# Results for one model ("elastic_net", "linear_svm"), connectivity type ("SFC", "FC", "SC") and feature set ("t1", "t1_slope")
en <- function(type, features, model = "elastic_net") {
  en_models[en_models$model == model & en_models$connectivity_type == type & en_models$features == features, ]
}

# Elastic net vs SVM feature importance agreement for one feature set ("t1", "t1_slope")
agreement <- function(features) en_svm_agreement[en_svm_agreement$features == features, ]

# Inline stats for one elastic net model
fmt_auc <- function(x) {
  f3 <- function(v) formatC(v, format = "f", digits = 3)
  paste0("AUC=", f3(x$auc), ", 95% CI ", f3(x$ci_low), " to ", f3(x$ci_high),
         ", p", fmt_p(x$p_value, 3), ", pFDR", fmt_p(x$p_fdr, 3), ", ", x$n_perm, " permutations")
}

### Derived demographic stats ###

# Look up a cell from the demographics table (built by demographics_table.py)
demo_cell <- function(variable, column, section = "") {
  demographics_table[[column]][demographics_table$Variable == variable & demographics_table$Section == section]
}

# Demographics table p-value formatted for inline text
demo_p <- function(variable, section = "") {
  p <- demo_cell(variable, "p_value", section)
  if (startsWith(p, "<")) p else paste0("=", p)
}

pct_sa <- round(as.numeric(demo_cell("N", "Superager")) / as.numeric(demo_cell("N", "Whole cohort")) * 100, 1)
### Derived model stats ###

# Main atlas results
res <- lme_results[[MAIN_ATLAS]]

# Min p-value or pFDR across networks, excluding any reported separately
min_stat <- function(fits, stat, exclude = character(0)) {
  min(sapply(fits[setdiff(names(fits), exclude)], `[[`, stat), na.rm = TRUE)
}

min_sfc_slope_p <- min_stat(res$group_change, "p_value")
min_sfc_slope_p_fdr <- min_stat(res$group_change, "p_fdr")
min_ravlt_slope_p <- min_stat(res$memory_change, "p_value", exclude = "salience")
min_ravlt_slope_p_fdr <- min_stat(res$memory_change, "p_fdr", exclude = "salience")
fmt_round2 <- function(p) formatC(round(p, 2), format = "f", digits = 2)

# Supplementary atlas results
res_s400 <- lme_results$schaefer400
```

Our overall cohort included `r demo_cell("N", "Whole cohort")` participants: `r demo_cell("Female, n (%)", "Whole cohort")` were female with a mean (range) baseline age of `r demo_cell("Age", "Whole cohort range", "Baseline")` years. `r pct_sa`% of the cohort met longitudinal superager criteria (see `r ref("flow")` for more details). Superagers and typical older adults did not vary on age at baseline (p`r demo_p("Age", "Baseline")`) or follow-up (p`r demo_p("Age", "Follow-up")`), years of education (p`r demo_p("Education (years)")`), baseline MMSE scores (p`r demo_p("MMSE", "Baseline")`), or follow-up duration (p`r demo_p("Follow-up duration (years)", "Follow-up")`); however, superagers were more likely to be female (p`r demo_p("Female, n (%)")`) and had higher MMSE scores at follow-up (p`r demo_p("MMSE", "Follow-up")`). These demographic statistics are summarized in `r ref("demographics")`.

```{r table1, results='asis'}
n_row <- demographics_table[demographics_table$Variable == "N", ]
demo <- demographics_table[demographics_table$Variable != "N", ]

# Headings are the only rows with no data
is_heading <- demo$`Whole cohort` == ""
is_section <- is_heading & demo$Variable == demo$Section
# Rows below a subsection heading (e.g. cognition) sit one level deeper
in_subsection <- ave(as.integer(is_heading & !is_section), demo$Section, FUN = cumsum) > 0
level <- ifelse(demo$Section == "" | is_section, 0, ifelse(is_heading | !in_subsection, 1, 2))

tbl1 <- demo[c("Variable", "Whole cohort", "Non-superager", "Superager", "p_value")]
names(tbl1) <- c("Variable",
                 sprintf("Whole cohort (n=%s)", n_row$`Whole cohort`),
                 sprintf("Typical older adults (n=%s)", n_row$`Non-superager`),
                 sprintf("Superagers (n=%s)", n_row$Superager),
                 "p-value")

ft <- style_rows(base_table(tbl1, "lrrrr"), tbl1$Variable, is_heading, level)
for (i in which(is_heading)) ft <- merge_h_range(ft, i = i, j1 = 1, j2 = ncol(tbl1))
finish_table(ft, caption_title("demographics", "Participant characteristics"))
```

::: {.note}
Values are mean (SD) or n (%), except age and MMSE, which are mean (range).
&dagger;Used to classify superagers; group differences on these measures are expected by design.
Abbreviations: MMSE, Mini-Mental State Examination;
RAVLT, Rey Auditory Verbal Learning Test; SD, standard deviation.
:::

**Machine learning elastic net models:** We calculated SFC as the correlation between each region's structural connectivity – measured through whole-brain tractography – and functional connectivity – measured as resting-state timeseries correlations (Figure 1; details in Methods). We used SFC, structural connectivity, and functional connectivity as features in separate elastic net classification models predicting superager status. Only SFC significantly predicted superager status in both the baseline (`r fmt_auc(en("SFC", "t1"))`) and baseline plus annual change (`r fmt_auc(en("SFC", "t1_slope"))`) models. Neither the functional connectivity baseline (`r fmt_auc(en("FC", "t1"))`) nor baseline plus annual change (`r fmt_auc(en("FC", "t1_slope"))`) models were significant, nor were the structural connectivity baseline (`r fmt_auc(en("SC", "t1"))`) or baseline plus annual change (`r fmt_auc(en("SC", "t1_slope"))`) models (`r ref("en_models")`). Permutation counts show how many shuffled-label models we ran before 50 matched or exceeded the model's AUC, indicating non-significance. The maximum number of possible permutations was 1,000. The top SFC features selected by permutation-based feature importance were broadly distributed across networks in both the baseline and baseline plus annual change models (`r ref("en_importance")`; `r ref("en_features")`). We repeated the analyses with a second machine learning model, a linear support vector machine, and found the same pattern: only SFC significantly predicted superager status in both the baseline and baseline plus annual change models (`r ref("en_svm")`). SFC feature importance was also strongly correlated between the two models (`r ref("en_svm_importance")`).

```{r table_en, results='asis'}
CONNECTIVITY_LABELS <- c(SFC = "Structure-function coupling", FC = "Functional connectivity", SC = "Structural connectivity")
FEATURE_LABELS <- c(t1 = "Baseline", t1_slope = "Baseline + annual change")
f3 <- function(v) formatC(v, format = "f", digits = 3)

# One data row per model ("elastic_net", "linear_svm")
model_row <- function(type, features, model) {
  x <- en(type, features, model)
  list(Model          = FEATURE_LABELS[[features]],
       `AUC (95% CI)` = paste0(f3(x$auc), " (", f3(x$ci_low), "-", f3(x$ci_high), ")"),
       `p-value`      = fmt_p_star(x$p_value, 3),
       pFDR           = fmt_p_star(x$p_fdr, 3),
       Permutations   = as.character(x$n_perm))
}

# Connectivity type heading, then its baseline and annual change rows
model_table <- function(model) {
  bind_rows(lapply(names(CONNECTIVITY_LABELS), function(type) {
    bind_rows(list(Model = CONNECTIVITY_LABELS[[type]], `AUC (95% CI)` = "", `p-value` = "", pFDR = "", Permutations = ""),
              lapply(names(FEATURE_LABELS), model_row, type = type, model = model))
  }))
}

render_sectioned_table(model_table("elastic_net"), "lrrrr", caption_title("en_models", "Elastic net models predicting superager status"))
```

::: {.note}
AUC confidence intervals are DeLong intervals on out-of-fold predictions. p-values are from permutation tests, with FDR correction across the six models.
Permutations show how many shuffled-label models were run before 50 matched or exceeded the model's AUC, indicating non-significance. The maximum number of possible permutations was 1,000.
\* p < 0.05, \*\* p < 0.01, \*\*\* p < 0.001.
Abbreviations: AUC, area under the curve; CI, confidence interval; FDR, false discovery rate.
:::

```{r figure-en-importance, results='asis'}
fig_title("en_importance", "Structure-function coupling feature importance in elastic net models")
single_figure(paste0("feature_importance_brain_", MAIN_ATLAS, ".png"), "80%")
```

::: {.note}
The 20 most important structure-function coupling features in the baseline (A) and baseline plus annual change (B) elastic net models, ranked by permutation importance. Colors indicate the network each feature belongs to. Hashed bars in (B) denote annual change features. Numbers in parentheses indicate the index of each region within its network in the Schaefer atlas. (C) Regions of each network shown on the Schaefer and subcortical atlases.
Abbreviations: LH, left hemisphere; PCC, posterior cingulate cortex; PFC, prefrontal cortex; R, right; RH, right hemisphere.
:::

**Structure-function coupling, superager status, and episodic memory:** We next used repeated-measures linear mixed-effects models to examine whether SFC varied longitudinally by superager status at the global and network levels. Superagers showed higher SFC than typical older adults globally (`r fmt_stats(res$group$global)`), in heteromodal regions (`r fmt_stats(res$group$hmod)`), and in memory-relevant networks including the DMN (`r fmt_stats(res$group$dmn)`), ECN (`r fmt_stats(res$group$control)`), and SN (`r fmt_stats(res$group$salience)`). By contrast, SFC in sensory regions did not differ by superager status (p`r fmt_p(res$group$sensory$p_value)`, pFDR`r fmt_p_fdr(res$group$sensory)`). `r ref("sfc_em")`A presents the difference in global SFC between superagers and typical older adults averaged across baseline and follow-up, with warmer colors indicating higher SFC in superagers, and `r ref("sfc_em")`B summarizes these results.

```{r figure-sfc-em, results='asis'}
fig_title("sfc_em", "Structure-function coupling, episodic memory, and superagers status analyses")
single_figure(paste0("em_sfc_cortex_plot_", MAIN_ATLAS, ".png"), "100%")
```

::: {.note}
(A) Cortical surface and subcortical plot of the unthresholded mean difference in global structure-function coupling between superagers and typical older adults, averaged across both timepoints. Warm colors indicate higher coupling in superagers; cool colors indicate lower coupling. (B, C) Linear mixed-effects model coefficients and 95% confidence intervals for regional structure-function coupling as a function of superager status (B) and episodic memory (C). Filled circles: p < .05 (uncorrected), open circles: non-significant, * pFDR < .05. Abbreviations: FDR, false discovery rate; SFC, structure-function coupling; DMN, default mode network; ECN, executive control network; SN, salience network; CI, confidence interval.
:::

We next examined the relationship between global and network level SFC and episodic memory across the cohort longitudinally with linear mixed-effects models. Higher SFC was associated with better episodic memory globally (`r fmt_stats(res$memory$global)`), in heteromodal regions (`r fmt_stats(res$memory$hmod)`), and in the DMN (`r fmt_stats(res$memory$dmn)`). The association in the ECN was nominally significant (`r fmt_stats(res$memory$control)`), and the SN showed a trend (`r fmt_stats(res$memory$salience)`). SFC in sensory regions was not associated with episodic memory (p`r fmt_p(res$memory$sensory$p_value)`, pFDR`r fmt_p_fdr(res$memory$sensory)`). `r ref("sfc_em")`C displays these results.

We next examined whether global and network level SFC change – modeled as an interaction with time in linear mixed-effects models – differed by superager status or was associated with episodic memory. We found no evidence that superager status was associated with SFC change in any network (ps ≥ `r fmt_round2(min_sfc_slope_p)`, pFDRs ≥ `r fmt_round2(min_sfc_slope_p_fdr)`). SFC change in the SN was weakly associated with episodic memory, but this did not survive correction for multiple comparisons (`r fmt_stats(res$memory_change$salience)`), and SFC change in other networks was not associated with episodic memory (ps ≥ `r fmt_round2(min_ravlt_slope_p)`, pFDRs ≥ `r fmt_round2(min_ravlt_slope_p_fdr)`). `r ref("lme")` summarizes all structure-function coupling, superager status, and episodic memory results.

We found similar results using the higher-resolution Schaefer 400 parcellation (`r ref("lme_s400")`). Superagers showed higher SFC than typical older adults in the ECN, which survived correction for multiple comparisons, with nominally significant effects in heteromodal regions and the SN, and trends globally and in the DMN. Higher SFC was associated with better episodic memory globally, in heteromodal regions, the DMN, and the SN, with a nominally significant association in the ECN. As in the main analysis, SFC in sensory regions neither differed by superager status nor was associated with episodic memory, and SFC change was not associated with superager status or episodic memory.

```{r table2, results='asis'}
# Helpers to build data rows for LME models
lme_row <- function(region, model) {
  list(
    Region                 = region,
    `Coefficient (95% CI)` = fmt_coef_ci(model),
    `p-value`              = fmt_p_star(as.numeric(model$p_value)[1]),
    pFDR                   = fmt_p_star(model$p_fdr),
    `Marginal r²`     = fmt_r2m(model),
    `Conditional r²`  = fmt_r2c(model)
  )
}

# Section header row (spans all columns via merge_at below)
hdr_row <- function(label) {
  list(Region = label, `Coefficient (95% CI)` = "",
       `p-value` = "", pFDR = "",
       `Marginal r²` = "", `Conditional r²` = "")
}

# Section type row (model description label, styled differently from hdr_row)
type_row <- function(label) {
  list(Region = label, `Coefficient (95% CI)` = "",
       `p-value` = "", pFDR = "",
       `Marginal r²` = "", `Conditional r²` = "")
}

NETWORK_LABELS <- c(
  global = "Global SFC", hmod = "Heteromodal SFC", dmn = "DMN SFC",
  control = "ECN SFC", salience = "SN SFC", sensory = "Sensory SFC"
)

type_labels <- c(
  "Repeated measures linear mixed-effects analyses",
  "Repeated measures linear mixed-effects analyses — change"
)

# Type and header rows, then one row per network
lme_section <- function(fits, type_label, header, suffix = "") {
  bind_rows(
    type_row(type_label),
    hdr_row(header),
    bind_rows(Map(function(fit, net) lme_row(paste0(NETWORK_LABELS[[net]], suffix), fit), fits, names(fits)))
  )
}

# All LME results for one atlas
lme_table <- function(res) {
  bind_rows(
    lme_section(res$group, type_labels[1], "Superager status"),
    lme_section(res$group_change, type_labels[2], "Superager status", " × time"),
    lme_section(res$memory, type_labels[1], "Episodic memory"),
    lme_section(res$memory_change, type_labels[2], "Episodic memory", " × time")
  )
}

# Headings italic and full width, network rows indented below them
render_lme_table <- function(tbl, title) {
  is_heading <- tbl$`Coefficient (95% CI)` == ""
  level <- ifelse(tbl$Region %in% type_labels, 0, ifelse(is_heading, 1, 2))
  ft <- style_rows(base_table(tbl, "lrrrrr"), tbl$Region, is_heading, level)
  for (i in which(is_heading)) ft <- merge_h_range(ft, i = i, j1 = 1, j2 = ncol(tbl))
  finish_table(ft, title)
}

render_lme_table(lme_table(res), caption_title("lme", "Associations between structure-function coupling, superager status, and episodic memory"))
```

::: {.note}
Models adjust for time, baseline age, sex, and years of education, with a random intercept per participant.
\* p < 0.05, \*\* p < 0.01, \*\*\* p < 0.001.
Abbreviations: CI, confidence interval; DMN, default mode network; ECN, executive control network;
FDR, false discovery rate; SFC, structure-function coupling; SN, salience network.
:::

## Supplementary material

### Functional magnetic resonance imaging motion

We excluded 33 participants for excessive head motion (more than 30% of volumes exceeding 0.5 mm framewise displacement): 21 at baseline and 22 at follow-up, with 10 excluded at both. Superagers and typical older adults did not differ significantly in mean framewise displacement or volumes scrubbed at baseline or follow-up (`r ref("motion")`).

```{r table_motion, results='asis'}
render_sectioned_table(motion_table, "lrrrr", caption_title("motion", "Head motion during resting-state fMRI at baseline and follow-up"))
```

::: {.note}
Values are mean (SD). P-values are from Welch t-tests.
Abbreviations: fMRI, functional magnetic resonance imaging; SD, standard deviation.
:::

### Linear support vector machine models

```{r table_svm, results='asis'}
render_sectioned_table(model_table("linear_svm"), "lrrrr", caption_title("en_svm", "Linear support vector machine models predicting superager status"))
```

::: {.note}
AUC confidence intervals are DeLong intervals on out-of-fold predictions. p-values are from permutation tests, with FDR correction across the six models.
Permutations show how many shuffled-label models were run before 50 matched or exceeded the model's AUC, indicating non-significance. The maximum number of possible permutations was 1,000.
\* p < 0.05, \*\* p < 0.01, \*\*\* p < 0.001.
Abbreviations: AUC, area under the curve; CI, confidence interval; FDR, false discovery rate.
:::

SFC feature importance was strongly correlated between the elastic net and linear support vector machine models in both the baseline (Spearman ρ=`r fmt_round2(agreement("t1")$spearman_rho)`) and baseline plus annual change (ρ=`r fmt_round2(agreement("t1_slope")$spearman_rho)`) models (`r ref("en_svm_importance")`). Of the `r agreement("t1")$top_n` most important SFC features in each model, `r agreement("t1")$top_n_shared` were shared in the baseline model and `r agreement("t1_slope")$top_n_shared` in the baseline plus annual change model.

```{r figure-en-svm-importance, results='asis'}
fig_title("en_svm_importance", "SFC feature importance in the elastic net and linear support vector machine models")
single_figure(paste0("en_svm_importance_", MAIN_ATLAS, ".png"), "100%")
```

::: {.note}
Each point is one SFC feature, colored by network. Filled points are baseline features and open points are annual change features. The dashed line marks equal importance in both models. Labels show the five most important features in the elastic net model, with parcel numbers in parentheses.
Abbreviations: AUC, area under the curve; LH, left hemisphere; RH, right hemisphere; SFC, structure-function coupling; SVM, support vector machine.
:::
